questions.q: Which function is pure?
questions.explain: Only the third depends on nothing but its parameters and changes nothing. The first reads a changeable variable, the second reads the clock (a hidden input), and the fourth mutates its argument (a hidden output).
options: const fee = (kobo) => kobo * config.feeRate; where config is a module variable that can change

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The function changes the prices inside the cart, so the second call discounts the already-discounted price. Same argument, different result: the mutation is a hidden output that becomes a hidden input next time.

questions.q: What does referential transparency mean?
questions.explain: If vat(1000) always returns 75 and does nothing else, every vat(1000) could be replaced by 75. That only holds for pure functions.
options: A function can see all variables in the program
A call can be replaced by its result anywhere without changing what the program does
A function returns a reference instead of a copy

questions.q: A delivery fee depends on the time of the order. What is the functional way to make it testable?
questions.explain: Turning the hidden input into a parameter makes the function pure. Production passes new Date(); tests pass fixed dates, including the exact boundary.
options: Pass the order time in as a parameter; the caller reads the clock
Run the tests at the right time of day

questions.q: In a "functional core, imperative shell" design, where does saving the order to the database go?
questions.explain: Effects are the program's purpose, so they stay, but at the edges. The core computes; the shell reads, calls the core, and writes.
options: In the core, next to the pricing rules
In the shell, which gathers inputs, calls the pure core, and performs the effects with its result
Nowhere: functional programs cannot save data
In every step of the pipeline

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only objects on the path to the change are new: the cart, the lines array and the oil line. The customer and the rice line are reused: that is structural sharing.

questions.q: This update was meant to be immutable. What does it print?
questions.explain: Spread copies one level. moved.address is the same object as order.address, so changing it changes the original. The immutable version is { ...order, address: { ...order.address, city: "Abuja" } }.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toSorted and with return copies and leave the original alone. with(1, …) replaces the item at index 1.

questions.q: Why is orders.reduce((acc, o) => ({ ...acc, [o.id]: o }), {}) slow for 50,000 orders?
questions.explain: Step 1 copies 0 entries, step 2 copies 1, …, step n copies n-1: about n²/2 copies. Mutating a local object or Map that nobody else can see yet is still pure from the caller's point of view, and O(n).
options: reduce is always slower than a loop
Every step copies all entries collected so far, so the total work grows with the square of the number of orders

questions.q: Is this function pure? function ids(orders) { const out = []; for (const o of orders) out.push(o.id); return out; }
questions.explain: Purity is about what callers can observe. Local mutation of fresh data is invisible outside the function, so the function is still pure.
options: Yes: it only mutates an array it created itself, which nobody can see until it returns
No, because it uses a loop

questions.q: Promotions are stored as an array of { name, discount(order) } objects instead of an if chain inside the checkout. What is the main benefit?
questions.explain: Treating rules as data (an array of functions) separates what the rules are from how they are applied. Tests and feature flags can pass different lists.
options: Rules can be added, removed, switched off and tested one at a time without changing the checkout code
Arrays use less memory than if statements
It removes the need for tests

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: pipe runs left to right: double then add ten (20). compose runs right to left: add ten then double (30), like the nested call double(addTen(5)).

questions.q: A ₦2,000 voucher (200000 kobo) and 7.5% VAT on a ₦17,000 order. What does this print?
questions.explain: Voucher first: VAT is charged on ₦15,000, total 1612500. VAT first: 1827500 minus the voucher, 1627500. The customer pays ₦150 less when the voucher comes off first. The order of steps is a business rule.

questions.q: Why must every step in a pipe take exactly one argument?
questions.explain: Data flows from one return value into the next call. Extra settings, such as a VAT rate, are fixed in advance with currying or partial application.
options: Because arrow functions cannot take more than one argument
Each step receives only the previous step's return value, and a function returns one value
It is a style rule with no technical reason

questions.q: What is the difference between currying and partial application?
questions.explain: Curried functions make partial application trivial (call with the first argument), but you can partially apply any function with bind or a partial helper.
options: Currying turns f(a, b, c) into f(a)(b)(c), one argument per call; partial application fixes some arguments now and returns a function of the rest
Partial application changes the original function

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Calling the curried function with only the rate returns the next function. Supplying the amount then gives the number.

questions.q: You want discount to be usable in pipe(discount(10), addVat). Which signature fits?
questions.explain: Configuration first, data last. The percent is known when the pipeline is built; the amount arrives when it runs.

questions.q: A generic curry uses fn.length. What does this print?
questions.explain: length counts parameters up to the first one with a default, and a rest parameter is not counted. That is why a generic curry calls such functions too early.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: bind(null, 100000, 20000) fixes the first two arguments. Math.ceil(1.2) is 2 kg, so 100000 + 2 × 20000 = 140000.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: map passes (item, index, array), so the calls are parseInt("7", 0) (guess: 7), parseInt("7", 1) (invalid radix: NaN) and parseInt("7", 2) (7 is not a binary digit: NaN). Write map((s) => parseInt(s, 10)) or map(Number).

questions.q: Why does skus.forEach(cart.add) fail when add uses this.items?
questions.explain: This is the lost-this problem from this in depth. Wrap it ((sku) => cart.add(sku)) or bind it.
options: Passing cart.add passes only the function; forEach calls it without an object, so this is undefined
Point-free style is not allowed with arrays

questions.q: When is point-free style (orders.filter(isPaid)) a good choice?
questions.explain: With your own single-argument functions it reads well and is safe. With functions that have optional extra parameters, or methods, wrap them in an arrow.
options: Always; arrow wrappers are never needed
When the function was written to take exactly the one argument being passed and does not use this

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: tap runs a side effect and passes its input through unchanged, so it can log the middle of a pipeline without changing the result.

questions.q: The checkout validates SKUs with Object.hasOwn(catalog, sku) rather than catalog[sku] !== undefined. Which SKU does that stop?
questions.explain: catalog.toString is the inherited method, not undefined, so the weaker check would accept it as a product. Object.hasOwn only accepts keys the catalog itself has.
options: "toString", which exists on every object through the prototype chain

questions.q: A request sends { sku: "TV-32", qty: 1, priceKobo: 1 }. Why does the lesson's priceLines ignore priceKobo?
questions.explain: Never trust money values from the outside. The pure core takes the catalog as an input, and always prices from it.
options: Because the field name is wrong
Prices must come from the server's catalog; a price sent by the client can be anything the client wants
Because 1 kobo is too small to charge

questions.q: Which test best shows that the checkout core does not mutate its input?
questions.explain: Freezing turns silent mutation into an error, and comparing the input afterwards confirms it. Running it twice and comparing results checks the "same input, same output" half.
options: Check that the total is correct
Deep-freeze the input, run the core (a mutation would throw), and check that the input still equals its original value
Check that it returns an object

questions.q: Why does the checkout keep every amount in whole kobo and round each calculated amount once?
questions.explain: Floating-point fractions accumulate errors. Integer minor units, rounded at agreed points, keep money exact and reproducible.
options: So every step works with exact integers and the totals match the invoice lines; rounding at random points makes totals drift by a kobo or two
Because rounding is a side effect

questions.q: Make deliveryFeeKobo pure: it must take the order time as a parameter instead of reading the clock. Evening orders (18:00 UTC or later) cost 150000, others 100000.
questions.explain: The clock was a hidden input. As a parameter, the boundary can be tested exactly, at any time of day.

questions.q: Write setQty(cart, sku, qty) that returns a new cart with that line's quantity changed, without changing the original, and reuses the lines that did not change.
questions.explain: Copy the objects on the path to the change (cart, lines array, the changed line) and reuse everything else. The frozen input proves nothing was mutated.

questions.q: Write pipe(...fns), which returns a function that passes its input through each function from left to right. Use it to build label: take off a 200000 kobo voucher (not below 0), add 7.5% VAT (rounded), and format as ₦16125.00.
questions.explain: reduce threads the value through the functions in order, starting from the input. A voucher larger than the order leaves 0, not a negative amount.

questions.q: Write a curried percentOff(percent)(kobo) that rounds to whole kobo, and use it with map to apply 15% off to every price.
questions.explain: percentOff(15) returns a one-argument function, which is exactly what map needs. The argument known early (the percent) comes first.

questions.q: The form sends quantities as text. The code below turns them into numbers but prints [ 3, NaN, NaN ]. Fix it so each quantity is parsed in base 10.
questions.explain: map passes the index as the second argument, which parseInt treats as the radix. An arrow that passes only the text (and radix 10) fixes it; map(Number) would also work.

questions.q: Write bestDiscount(order, rules): each rule is a function from order to a discount in kobo. Return the largest discount, but never more than order.subtotalKobo, and 0 when there are no rules.
questions.explain: Rules are data: map them to amounts and keep the largest, starting from 0 so an empty list works. Capping at the subtotal means no rule, however wrong, can make a total negative.

questions.q: What does it mean that functions are first-class values in JavaScript?
questions.explain: First-class functions are what make callbacks, rule arrays, pipe, currying and factories possible.
options: They can be stored in variables and arrays, passed as arguments and returned from other functions, like any other value
They cannot be changed after they are declared

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Object.freeze is shallow: the order object is frozen, but the lines array and the line objects inside it are not. To use freezing as a mutation detector, freeze every level.
options: TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property

questions.q: An immutable removeLine(cart, sku) returns the original cart object when the SKU is not in it. Why is that useful?
questions.explain: With immutable data, a new object means something changed and the same object means nothing did. That makes change detection a single comparison.
options: It saves one line of code
Callers can detect "nothing changed" cheaply with ===, and caches or UIs can skip work

questions.q: When is a generic curry(fn) helper a poor choice?
questions.explain: curry decides when to call the function by counting arguments against fn.length. Defaults and rest parameters make that count wrong. Hand-written curried arrows are explicit and safer.
options: When the function has exactly two required parameters
When the function has default or rest parameters, because fn.length no longer tells how many arguments it needs
When the function returns a number

questions.q: In the lesson's checkout shell, saveOrder, log and clock are passed in as functions. What does that give you?
questions.explain: The shell is still impure, but its effects are injected, so they are visible and replaceable. In a ZudoJS service, the container provides them.
options: The shell can run in a test with fakes (an array for saving, a fixed clock), and production passes the real ones; nothing in the shell reaches for globals
It removes the need for the core

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: compose applies the rightmost function first, like the nested form c(b(a(x))).

questions.q: Write partial(fn, ...preset) that returns a function which calls fn with the preset arguments followed by the new ones. Use it to fix the zone table of shippingKobo.
questions.explain: A rest parameter collects the preset arguments, the returned arrow collects the rest, and spread passes them all in order. It is bind without the this argument.
